body.text: According to a statement issued by Pakistan’s Foreign Office, the discussions centered on advancing trade, investment, regional connectivity, agricultural modernization, and people-to-people exchanges. Dar also stressed the need for sustained high-level engagements to advance what the Pakistani officials describe as a “Pakistan-China Community of Shared Future in the New Era.” The meeting comes as both countries seek to fast-track the second phase of CPEC.
It appears to be part of the two countries’ ongoing effort to accelerate CPEC-related work and clarify the project’s second phase.

Phase one of the project is known for largely delivering energy projects, roads, and basic connectivity infrastructure. Phase two, on the other hand, is expected to emphasize industrial cooperation, mining, critical minerals, agriculture, and technology. Moreover, information sharing and people-to-people exchanges, long described as pillars of the corridor’s long-term vision, along with opening the mineral sector, are increasingly framed as part of the second phase.
On the ground, the path being taken to accelerate the second phase already looks different from the large-scale infrastructure focus that defined the early years of development.

Pakistan and China recently launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor (CPIC), to counter what officials have called “misleading narratives,” expand cultural exchanges, and strengthen think tank cooperation.

From the Pakistani and Chinese perspectives, such narratives have often portrayed CPEC as little more than a debt burden or a strategic liability rather than a development partnership. The new information corridor, it seems, is intended to present a more coordinated account of the relationship. Moreover, a closer think tank engagement could, in principle, help policymakers in both countries better align priorities and reduce the informational friction that has occasionally complicated implementation. In that sense, CPIC seems linked to the practical needs of CPEC rather than standing apart from them.

In his address to inaugurate CPIC, Pakistan’s Information Minister Ataullah Tarar captured the intended shift when he observed that the first phase of CPEC connected lands, while the next would “connect our minds.” He said the information corridor will act as a bridge between the peoples of the two countries.

Arguably, this renewed emphasis on information sharing and narrative alignment is based on the fact that public perceptions and policy coordination matter as much as physical infrastructure at this stage.

Whether the issue of misinformation has undermined cooperation in the past remains open to debate. However, the decision to institutionalize fact-checking mechanisms and joint media working groups suggests that both countries now treat the issue as one that needs addressing now rather than deferred as a secondary concern.

Pakistan and China are also focusing on mapping, regulating, and opening Pakistan’s mineral sector, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province. CPEC’s phase two is expected to prioritize industrial cooperation, mining, and the excavation of critical minerals as well. Special economic zones, which are being set up, are more likely to succeed if the industries located in them can process local resources rather than simply assemble or package imported inputs.

In this regard, Rashakai Special Economic Zone (RSEZ) in KP offers a useful illustration of such cooperation between Pakistan and China. The project is operated through a joint venture involving the China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Economic Zone and Management Company. The SEZ was designed from the outset around value-addition industries, with mineral processing listed among its core designated sectors.

Provincial authorities in KP have recently intensified this message, particularly on mineral extraction and refining in the province. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi recently said that the province’s mineral resources would be extracted and sold to promote economic prosperity. He urged foreign companies to invest through joint ventures.

The timing of Kundi’s statement is particularly notable. The renewed emphasis on mineral governance comes amid a recent provincial leadership change in KP following the imposition of governor’s rule, which has shifted administrative authority from the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)-led provincial government to the federal government. Under this arrangement, Islamabad could now exercise more influence over provincial regulatory affairs, including strategic mineral assets.
This administrative shift has temporarily softened long-standing frictions between the federal and provincial governments over resource management and joint investment frameworks.

These developments point to a CPEC phase that appears to be less about infrastructure and more about information coordination, industrial networks, and the organized development of Pakistan’s mineral base.

Similarly, the approach of Pakistan and China in the second phase is different from the first phase as it appears to rest on the idea that closer policy alignment and people-to-people understanding will make the economic partnership under CPEC more viable over the long run.
